items.title: The ocean's most abundant 'loner' microbe has a sticky second life
items.desc: The oxygen in about every other breath we take comes from microscopic cells—phytoplankton—drifting in the surface of the ocean. Among them is Prochlorococcus, the smallest and most abundant photosynthetic organism in the seas. It single-handedly accounts for roughly 10% of all the carbon that the land and the oceans pull from the atmosphere each year.

items.title: Tackling Lake Erie's algal blooms requires targeted conservation strategies
items.desc: Anyone living along the coast of Lake Erie will be well aware of the periodic algal blooms that appear on its surface. The greenish blooms can cause rashes and other health problems and pose risks to both humans and animals.

items.title: Genomes of 20 eastern Finnish species provide unique insights into species' adaptations to local conditions
items.desc: In recent years, researchers at the University of Eastern Finland have been both leading and contributing to collaborative genome projects. These efforts have produced reference-quality genome assemblies for the Finnish brown hare and the mountain hare, as well as the Saimaa ringed seal, in collaboration with research partners.

items.title: Parents and nongamers struggle to identify video game loot boxes
items.desc: New research has found parents, guardians and nongamers may struggle to recognize video game loot boxes, their defining features and the digital receipts linked to purchases.

items.title: Atomic memory keeps distant ions entangled for about 10 seconds
items.desc: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices and allow them to exchange information encoded in the quantum states of particles, could enable more secure communications. To build these networks, physicists need to devise strategies that allow distant particles to share quantum states, preserving them long enough to perform calculations or enable communication between devices.

items.title: Smart planning of outdoor sports tournaments using environmental heat measurements
items.desc: Rising temperatures caused by climate change are making it harder to organize outdoor sports events safely. Exercising in the heat lowers performance and raises the risk of heatstroke, which is a leading cause of nontraumatic death among professional athletes.

items.title: Can surplus-food apps have too much competition?
items.desc: Apps that let businesses sell surplus food at a discount in "surplus bags" have become a popular way to keep edible food out of landfills while giving consumers access to lower-cost meals and groceries.

items.title: Q&A: Do new platform features hurt hiring chances for competitive gig workers?
items.desc: Whether they are driven by economic necessity or a desire for greater control over their careers, a growing number of workers are turning to online gig-work platforms to supplement their income with freelance projects like coding or website design.

items.title: Synchronized bodily responses do not always reflect cooperation, study finds
items.desc: Sometimes, while people are interacting with each other, their movements and physiological responses can fall into step. Some past studies have linked synchronized bodily responses to cooperation and being attuned to the emotions of others.

items.title: South Korea launches new bid to guide crowd-pulling shark to sea
items.desc: South Korean authorities began a new attempt Wednesday to coax a shark-turned-viral sensation back to sea, with falling temperatures in the Busan canal where it is stranded raising concerns for its survival.

items.title: Prized wild pepper at risk in Madagascar's shrinking forests
items.desc: A rare wild pepper endemic to Madagascar and prized by international chefs is facing an uncertain future, a victim of its own success and the destruction of its forest habitat.

items.title: More current with less calcium: Computational models help solve longstanding ion channel evolution mystery
items.desc: In the early 1980s, scientists observed an anomaly. Embedded within cell membranes, they identified ion channels with extraordinarily high conductance. These so-called "BK" (Big K, or Big Potassium) channels had roughly 10 times the unitary conductance (i.e., conductance per individual channel molecule) of other potassium channels, enabling much more efficient, rapid transport of potassium ions. And while later structural characterization explained how this happened, no one could understand why. That is, until now.

items.title: Transparent minispheres reveal that some look-alike cancer drugs part ways in 3D
items.desc: Researchers at Uppsala University have adapted Cell Painting, a widely used imaging method in drug discovery, to look at individual cells inside small 3D clusters of cancer cells. Two drugs that looked almost identical in ordinary flat cell cultures behaved differently in 3D, and the team linked the difference to how each drug switches on the cell's p53 stress response.

items.title: A First Nation community in Canada is using a data center to preserve its heritage
items.desc: For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data center to help preserve its heritage.

items.title: Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why statins, the widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs that help prevent heart attacks and strokes, can sometimes cause muscle pain, weakness, and even severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers discovered that statins can attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells and force open a channel that normally controls calcium flow. This causes calcium to leak continuously, potentially damaging muscle tissue.

items.title: Hurricane warning maps are improving, but a dangerous problem remains
items.desc: A new study reveals that improved hurricane forecast graphics may help people identify threatened areas without making them more likely to recognize the danger or take protective action. Researchers also found that a widespread misunderstanding of the hurricane cone persists, highlighting a potentially dangerous gap between accurate forecasts and public preparedness.

items.title: Astronomers uncover new secrets of the Universe’s first five minutes
items.desc: Scientists have achieved a major breakthrough in understanding the Universe’s earliest moments, measuring the amount of helium formed in the first five minutes after the Big Bang with unprecedented precision. Using one of the world’s most powerful telescopes, an international team studied 15 remarkably pristine galaxies that act as cosmic time capsules, preserving clues from nearly 13.8 billion years ago.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
items.desc: A surprising clinical trial suggests that taking vitamin C daily could improve survival in people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers. Patients receiving the supplement had fewer adverse events and showed a promising survival advantage, raising hopes that a common vitamin could help protect against leukemia-related complications.

items.title: Scientists discover a bizarre Jurassic “squid” unlike anything ever seen
items.desc: Scientists have identified the “fattest” belemnite ever discovered, a bizarre, barrel-shaped squid relative that lived in Wyoming’s ancient seas 160 million years ago. The exceptionally rare fossils reveal a creature unlike anything previously known, potentially a predator of smaller squid-like animals and a surprising survivor of a supposedly vanished family.

items.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable
items.desc: The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

items.title: Scientists find a way to fight Alzheimer’s brain damage without removing toxic tau
items.desc: Scientists have found a promising way to protect the brain from Alzheimer’s-related damage by blocking immune cells that contribute to the destruction of neurons. In mice, the treatment preserved roughly 40% more tissue in memory centers and improved memory, even without removing harmful tau protein buildup.

items.title: NASA solves a strange mystery hidden inside asteroid Bennu’s boulders
items.desc: NASA scientists have finally uncovered why asteroid Bennu loses heat so quickly despite being covered in massive boulders. Samples returned to Earth reveal that its rocks are filled with hidden cracks, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for years.

items.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
items.desc: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

items.title: Scientists reach the ultimate quantum limit on a surface
items.desc: Scientists have achieved a quantum breakthrough by creating an ultra-clean surface where individual molecules can maintain their delicate quantum properties at the fundamental limit. The discovery could unlock unprecedented control over molecules and help drive the next generation of quantum technologies.

items.title: NASA reveals 16 stunning galaxies hiding cosmic chaos
items.desc: NASA's stunning new gallery of 16 galaxies reveals colossal black hole jets, explosive star formation, and spectacular cosmic collisions through the combined power of Chandra, James Webb, Hubble, and other telescopes. These extraordinary images expose the hidden forces shaping galaxies across the universe and offer clues about the Milky Way's own past and future.

items.title: Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
items.desc: A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second-highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists discovered that the disaster was preceded by several warning signs, including rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall, and thousands of tiny seismic tremors. As glaciers retreat, similar disasters could become a growing danger in mountainous coastal regions.

items.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
items.desc: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.

items.title: Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people
items.desc: Scientists have discovered evidence of two hidden magma sources beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano, where satellite observations revealed mysterious ground movements suggesting magma is shifting deep underground. The findings could improve eruption forecasting for the active volcano, which sits near 2 million people and attracts tourists to its spectacular lava lake.

items.title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
items.desc: A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

items.title: What’s Driving Persistent Inflation?
items.desc: In their preoccupation with high public debt, rising bond yields, and dizzying AI valuations, investors have seemingly forgotten the supply shocks shaping the underlying inflation outlook. But anyone worried about debt and yields must reckon with the disruptions created in the name of protecting domestic markets.

items.title: Building the Economy Africa Needs
items.desc: Africa cannot control global geopolitics, let alone prevent external shocks. But it can manage its exposure, especially by building an integrated continental market, investing in higher-value-added production, and pushing for reform of the global credit-rating agencies.

items.title: Science Without Scientists?
items.desc: Now that autonomous systems are capable of generating their own hypotheses, designing experiments, and writing up the results, the scientific community must adapt. For scientific knowledge to retain its standing, its sources must be trusted and answerable to the public.

items.title: When Smart Cities Turn Menacing
items.desc: Uganda has embraced digital-surveillance tools in the name of improving public safety and combating terrorism, a pattern that is repeating itself across several African countries. But governments are increasingly using these technologies for political control, rather than for national security.

items.title: Brazil Cannot Afford Bolsonaro’s Spending Cuts
items.desc: If he wins the October 25 runoff, far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro plans to slash public spending by as much as 1.5% of GDP. These cuts could push Brazil into recession, hurt workers and small businesses, and drain tax revenue—all without solving the country’s debt problem.

items.title: A Generational Reckoning on the Streets of Paris
items.desc: As their schools deteriorate and the planet grows hotter, many young people in France do not have hope for a decent future. The recent protests may foreshadow a broader conflict between older generations who wield political power and younger people who must live in the world they leave behind.

items.title: The Algorithm Driving French Student Protests
items.desc: One of the main drivers of the student protests in France is the opposition to Parcoursup, the country’s university-admissions platform, which is widely denounced as opaque and unfair. While such automated decision-making systems do not create educational inequalities, they can exacerbate them.

items.title: PS Events: Reinventing Europe
items.desc: Despite boasting world-leading universities and research institutions, robust trade relationships, a strong industrial base, and a well-established rule of law, Europe has failed to leverage its advantages in a way that would unlock its full economic potential.

items.title: A Nobel for the Poor People’s Lawyer
items.desc: From growing up in a slum outside Durban to studying law in a segregated university, Navi Pillay’s experience in apartheid-era South Africa instilled in her a lifelong belief in the importance of international courts in defending people’s rights. Now she should use her newly won stature to advance the rule of law at home.

items.title: MAGA at the Acropolis
items.desc: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s ideologically loaded recent speech in Athens attempted to trace MAGA’s ideological roots back to ancient democracy. But emphasizing the West’s shared civilizational inheritance will not convince Europeans to embrace the hubris of the Trump administration’s imperial worldview.

items.title: Breathing New Life Into Organized Labor
items.desc: Fulfilling the International Labour Organization’s promise of defending workers’ rights will require more than another declaration or incremental institutional reform. Instead, there must be a concerted global effort to create an enabling environment for all workers and their organizations to operate across borders as easily as capital does.

items.title: The State That Remembers
items.desc: Although many economists believe that AI could drive an economic transformation larger than the Industrial Revolution, and on a vastly shorter timetable, most governments are unequipped to manage such a transition. We urgently need states that can learn on the go and remember what they learn.

items.title: The End of Abundance
items.desc: The decades ahead will be shaped by a contest for natural resources, making the world more prone to stagflation and handing the levers of policy back to governments. Emerging economies that are rich in people but poor in resources will be the most acutely affected but can take practical steps to strengthen their resilience.
